sections.section_title: The Thesis of the Letter's Second Movement
sections.summary: Paul declares that Christ set believers free for freedom and commands them to stand firm and not submit again to a yoke of slavery.
sections.relevance: The imperative 'stand firm' and the prohibition 'do not submit again to a yoke of slavery' presuppose that the freedom Christ won can be surrendered by the believers' own action. If the freedom were unconditionally guaranteed regardless of subsequent conduct, the command to hold it would be pointless. The word 'again' (palin) implies that resubmission to bondage is a real possibility for those who have been freed, indicating that the believer's liberated standing requires active maintenance rather than being automatically preserved.
key_phrases: For freedom Christ has set us free
do not submit again to a yoke of slavery

sections.section_title: The Consequences of Circumcision -- Severance and Obligation
sections.summary: Paul warns that accepting circumcision as a condition of justification renders Christ of no advantage, obligates to the whole law, severs from Christ, and constitutes falling from grace; he contrasts this with the path of waiting by the Spirit through faith for the hope of righteousness, where only faith working through love has force.
sections.relevance: This passage directly and unambiguously addresses whether a believer's standing before God can be lost. The neutral reading identifies three consequences for those who seek justification through the law: (1) Christ will be of no advantage (5:2); (2) they are severed from Christ (katergethete apo Christou, 5:4a) -- the verb katargeo describes the dissolution of a previously operative connection; (3) they have fallen from grace (tes charitos exepesate, 5:4b) -- the verb ekpipto describes departure from a position previously occupied. The neutral reading explicitly states: 'The calling that brought them into grace (1:6) can be abandoned; the sphere of grace can be departed.' The aorist tenses treat the severance and the fall as accomplished fact for anyone who takes this step. This is part of Paul's own sustained argument -- not an illustration, aside, or assumption -- and it directly describes a real mechanism by which believers can be cut off from Christ and relocated outside of grace through their own volitional reorientation.
key_phrases: if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you
obligated to keep the whole law
You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law
you have fallen away from grace

sections.summary: Paul describes the Galatians as having been running well before someone cut in to hinder them from obeying the truth, warns that the persuasion to adopt circumcision does not come from God who calls them, uses the leaven metaphor to show how small compromise transforms the whole, expresses confidence they will reject the false view, and wishes the agitators would emasculate themselves.
sections.relevance: The passage implies that believers who were on the right path can be diverted from it by external influence. The declaration that 'this persuasion is not from him who calls you' (5:8) distinguishes God's ongoing calling from the rival teaching, implying that believers can follow a persuasion that leads away from God. The leaven metaphor (5:9) warns that small compromise will transform the entire community's basis from faith to law, implying the community's standing is vulnerable to corruption from within.
key_phrases: You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth?
This persuasion is not from him who calls you
A little leaven leavens the whole lump

sections.section_title: Freedom Redefined -- Not License but Love
sections.summary: Paul exhorts the Galatians not to use their freedom as an opportunity for the flesh but to serve one another through love, declares that the whole law is fulfilled in the command to love one's neighbor as oneself, and warns against the mutual destruction of biting and devouring one another.

Paul commands the Galatians to walk by the Spirit with the promise that they will not fulfill the flesh's desires, describes the structural opposition between flesh and Spirit, and declares that those led by the Spirit are not under the law.

Paul lists the self-evident works of the flesh -- including sexual immorality, idolatry, enmity, strife, jealousy, divisions, and envy -- and warns the Galatians, as he had warned them before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
sections.relevance: The warning 'those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God' (5:21b) is addressed directly to believers -- the Galatian assemblies who were identified as heirs of the Abrahamic promise (3:29, 4:7). The present participle 'those who practice' (hoi prassontes) describes ongoing, habitual conduct rather than isolated incidents. The neutral reading states: 'The inheritance is real, but it can be forfeited by those who turn their freedom into a base of operations for the flesh.' This passage directly addresses whether the inheritance promised to believers is conditional on conduct, and it does so as part of Paul's own sustained argument within the flesh-Spirit framework of chapters 5-6. The warning is not hypothetical; it is addressed to the same people declared sons and heirs, indicating that heir-status does not automatically guarantee receipt of the inheritance.
key_phrases: those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God
I warn you, as I warned you before

sections.summary: Paul describes the singular fruit of the Spirit -- love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control -- and notes that against such things there is no law.

Paul declares that those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires, exhorts that those who live by the Spirit should keep in step with the Spirit, and warns against conceit, mutual provocation, and envy.
